### 2.6.8. Marker selection per cell type

When later performing statistical tests, we want to guide our attention to markers that are more likely to be truly positive signals rather than markers than show background signal. For a given cell type, e.g. CD4 T cells, we can assume that most B cell markers should not be present. Therefore, we want to identify markers that are mostly associated with background signal across each cell type, so that we can disregard them in downstream analyses. 

To identify such markers, we employ Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression, which allows us to model the relationship between isotype marker abundance and overall background signal in the dataset. The analysis is conducted separately for each cell type, allowing us to capture cell type-specific background patterns. The PLS model is fitted using isotype markers as predictors, and results in a background score describing the background level in each cell. Additionally, we obtain background loadings that indicate the contribution of each marker to the background signal. If a marker has a positive loading, it suggests that the marker is strongly associated with background signal in that cell type. For each cell type, we keep markers that either have a very high abundance (mean CLR > 10 isotype CLR std) or have medium abundance (mean CLR > 3 isotype CLR std) and a background PLS loading below 0.05. The markers that are retained in any condition will be used for downstream statistical testing.

We utilize the `isotype_pls` helper function to perform the PLS regression. The function takes as input the isotype markers, a model matrix to account for sample-level covariates, and options to specify the data layer and whether to remove covariate effects. The output includes both the background scores for each cell and the loadings for each marker.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_marker_selection

cell_annotation_column <-
  "cell_annotation"
isotype_markers <-
  c("mIgG1", "mIgG2a", "mIgG2b")


cell_data <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data,
    vars = c(cell_annotation_column)
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  group_by(cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column))

pls_fit_celltype <-
  cell_data |>
  group_split() |>
  set_names(group_keys(cell_data)$cell_type) |>
  lapply(function(cells) {
    pg_data |>
      subset(cells = cells$component) %>%
      isotype_pls(isotype_markers,
        model_mat = with(.[[]], model.matrix(~sample_alias)),
        layer = "scale.data",
        remove_covariates = TRUE
      )
  })


# Background scores

bg_scores <-
  pls_fit_celltype |>
  lapply(function(x) enframe(x$scores, "component", "bg_score")) |>
  bind_rows()

pg_data[[]] <-
  pg_data[[]] |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  left_join(bg_scores, by = "component") |>
  column_to_rownames("component")


FeaturePlot(
  pg_data,
  features = "bg_score"
) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry")) +
  labs(title = "Isotype background score")

export_plot(
  filename = here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_score_featureplot"),
  width = 6,
  height = 5
)

# Background loadings

bg_loadings <-
  pls_fit_celltype %>%
  lapply(function(x) enframe(x$loadings, "marker", "bg_loading")) |>
  bind_rows(.id = cell_annotation_column)

bg_loadings |>
  arrange(-bg_loading) |>
  mutate(marker = factor(marker, levels = unique(marker))) |>
  ggplot(aes(marker, !!sym(cell_annotation_column), fill = bg_loading)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry")) +
  labs(
    title = "PLS loadings for isotype markers",
    x = "Marker",
    fill = "PLS loading",
    y = "Cell type"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_loading_heatmap"),
  width = 15,
  height = 6
)


FetchData(pg_data,
  vars = isotype_markers,
  layer = "data"
) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  left_join(bg_scores, by = c("component")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(isotype_markers),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(abundance, bg_score)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>%
      group_by(marker) %>%
      summarise(cor = cor(abundance, bg_score)),
    aes(label = paste0("r = ", round(cor, 2))),
    x = Inf, y = -Inf,
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_grid(~marker, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Background score vs isotype marker abundance",
    x = "Marker abundance (CLR)",
    y = "Background score"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_score_vs_isotype_abundance"),
  width = 12,
  height = 5
)

isotype_levels <-
  FetchData(pg_data, c(
    "condition", cell_annotation_column,
    isotype_markers
  )) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  mutate(max_isotype = pmax(!!!syms(isotype_markers))) |>
  group_by(condition, !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  summarise(
    mean_isotype = mean(max_isotype),
    sd_isotype = sd(max_isotype)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

abundance_data_per_celltype <-
  FetchData(pg_data, c(
    "condition", cell_annotation_column,
    rownames(pg_data)
  )) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(rownames(pg_data)),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  group_by(condition, !!sym(cell_annotation_column), marker) |>
  summarise(
    mean_abundance = mean(abundance),
    sd_abundance = sd(abundance),
    n_cells = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(isotype_levels,
    by = c(
      "condition",
      cell_annotation_column
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(bg_loadings,
    by = c(
      "marker",
      cell_annotation_column
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_low = mean_abundance < mean_isotype + 3 * sd_isotype,
    is_high = mean_abundance > mean_isotype + 10 * sd_isotype,
    is_noisy = bg_loading > 0.05,
    passed_filter = case_when(
      is_low ~ "Not passed",
      is_high ~ "Passed",
      is_noisy ~ "Not passed",
      TRUE ~ "Passed"
    )
  )

abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  mutate(cell_annotation = !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  ggplot(aes((mean_abundance - mean_isotype) / sd_isotype, bg_loading,
    color = passed_filter
  )) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = marker), size = 2) +
  facet_grid(condition ~ cell_annotation) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Marker mean abundance vs PLS loading",
    x = "Mean abundance (CLR)",
    y = "PLS loading"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/marker_selection_scatterplot"),
  width = 15,
  height = 10
)

markers_per_cell_type <-
  abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  filter(passed_filter == "Passed") |>
  select(condition, cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column), marker) |>
  distinct() |>
  group_by(cell_type)

abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  mutate(cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  filter(passed_filter == "Passed") |>
  ggplot(aes(marker, condition)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_grid(cell_type ~ .) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Selected markers per cell type",
    x = "Marker",
    y = "Condition"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/selected_markers_heatmap"),
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)

markers_per_cell_type |>
  write_csv(here::here("results/02_data_processing/isotype_background_score/selected_markers.csv"))

markers_to_test <-
  markers_per_cell_type |>
  group_split() |>
  set_names(group_keys(markers_per_cell_type)$cell_type) |>
  lapply(function(df) unique(df$marker))
```

# 3. Abundance distribution

This section generates abundance distribution plots for a selected subset of markers in the dataset, providing detailed visualizations of marker expression patterns across different experimental dimensions. For each marker, plots are generated using both normalized CLR (centered log-ratio) values and raw count data, allowing users to assess expression patterns in both normalized and absolute terms.

The analysis creates multiple visualization perspectives to facilitate exploration:

- **Per sample**: Shows marker abundance distributions across all samples, useful for identifying sample-specific expression patterns or batch effects
- **Per cell type**: Displays marker expression within each annotated cell type, helping to identify cell type-specific markers and expression heterogeneity
- **Per cell type faceted by group**: Combines cell type and group information (by default: condition), enabling identification of group-specific expression differences per cell type; switch `abundance_plots_grouping_column` to `"sample_alias"` to facet by individual sample instead
- **Per condition faceted by cell type**: Compares marker abundance across experimental conditions within each cell type, useful for identifying condition-specific changes in marker expression

These visualizations are valuable for quality control, marker validation, and exploratory data analysis. They help identify markers with high variability, detect potential batch effects, and understand marker expression patterns across the experimental design.

**Note**: By default, only a selected subset of markers is plotted to keep runtime manageable. Adjust `markers_for_abundance_plots` to the markers relevant to your project.

```{r}
# Markers to generate abundance distribution plots for. Replace with the markers
# relevant to your project, e.g.: c("CD3e", "CD4", "CD8", "CD19", "CD56").
# By default the first 10 markers are used as a placeholder only.
# To plot all markers set: markers_for_abundance_plots <- rownames(pg_data)
markers_for_abundance_plots <- rownames(pg_data)[seq_len(min(10, nrow(pg_data)))]

# Column used to facet the "per cell type" plots. Set to "condition" (default) to
# facet by experimental condition, or "sample_alias" to facet by individual sample.
abundance_plots_grouping_column <- "sample_alias"

all_markers <- rownames(pg_data)

# Collect CLR and count data
plot_data_clr <- FetchData(pg_data, c("sample_alias", "cell_annotation", "condition", all_markers), layer = "data")
plot_data_cts <- FetchData(pg_data, c("sample_alias", "cell_annotation", "condition", all_markers), layer = "counts")

# concatenate CLR and count data
plot_data <- plot_data_clr |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(all_markers), names_to = "marker", values_to = "abundance") |>
  mutate(metric = "CLR") |>
  bind_rows(
    plot_data_cts |>
      pivot_longer(cols = all_of(all_markers), names_to = "marker", values_to = "abundance") |>
      mutate(metric = "Count")
  )

plot_data |>
  filter(marker %in% markers_for_abundance_plots) |>
  group_by(marker) |>
  group_map(~ {
    marker_savename <- str_remove(.y, "\\.") # remove dot from marker name for saving files
    # Create 2 plots for the current marker: CLR per sample, Count per sample
    p_clr_per_sample <- .x |> # .x contains the grouped data for the current marker
      filter(metric == "CLR") |>
      ggplot(aes(sample_alias, abundance, color = sample_alias)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
      labs(title = "CLR per sample", x = "", y = "CLR")

    # Set y limits to the 99th percentile per marker
    count_99 <- quantile(.x$abundance[.x$metric == "Count"], 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
    p_count_per_sample <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "Count") |>
      ggplot(aes(sample_alias, abundance, color = sample_alias)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
      labs(title = "Count per sample", x = "", y = "Count") +
      ylim(NA, count_99)

    # Save per sample plots
    p_abundance_distribution_per_sample <- (p_clr_per_sample + p_count_per_sample) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = paste0("Marker: ", .y)) # .y contains the name of the current marker
    export_plot(
      filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/03_abundance/abundance_plots/per_sample/{marker_savename}_abundance_distribution_per_sample")),
      width = 12,
      height = 8,
      plot = p_abundance_distribution_per_sample
    )

    # Create 2 plots for the current marker: CLR per cell type, Count per cell type
    p_clr_per_celltype <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "CLR") |>
      ggplot(aes(cell_annotation, abundance, color = cell_annotation)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
      labs(title = "CLR per cell type", x = "", y = "CLR")

    p_count_per_celltype <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "Count") |>
      ggplot(aes(cell_annotation, abundance, color = cell_annotation)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
      labs(title = "Count per cell type", x = "", y = "Count") +
      ylim(NA, count_99)

    # Save per cell type plots
    p_abundance_distribution_per_celltype <- (p_clr_per_celltype + p_count_per_celltype) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = paste0("Marker: ", .y)) # .y contains the name of the current marker
    export_plot(
      filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/03_abundance/abundance_plots/per_cell_type/{marker_savename}_abundance_distribution_per_celltype")),
      width = 12,
      height = 8,
      plot = p_abundance_distribution_per_celltype
    )

    # Save per cell type plots faceted by grouping column (default: condition;
    # change abundance_plots_grouping_column to "sample_alias" to facet by sample)
    p_clr_per_celltype_faceted_by_group <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "CLR") |>
      ggplot(aes(cell_annotation, abundance, color = cell_annotation)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
      labs(title = glue::glue("CLR per cell type faceted by {abundance_plots_grouping_column}"), x = "", y = "CLR") +
      facet_wrap(~ .data[[abundance_plots_grouping_column]])

    p_count_per_celltype_faceted_by_group <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "Count") |>
      ggplot(aes(cell_annotation, abundance, color = cell_annotation)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
      labs(title = glue::glue("Count per cell type faceted by {abundance_plots_grouping_column}"), x = "", y = "Count") +
      facet_wrap(~ .data[[abundance_plots_grouping_column]]) +
      ylim(NA, count_99)

    p_abundance_distribution_per_celltype_faceted_by_group <- (p_clr_per_celltype_faceted_by_group + p_count_per_celltype_faceted_by_group) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = paste0("Marker: ", .y)) # .y contains the name of the current marker
    export_plot(
      filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/03_abundance/abundance_plots/per_cell_type_faceted_by_{abundance_plots_grouping_column}/{marker_savename}_abundance_distribution_per_celltype_faceted_by_{abundance_plots_grouping_column}")),
      width = 16,
      height = 12,
      plot = p_abundance_distribution_per_celltype_faceted_by_group
    )

    # Create plots for the current marker: CLR per condition per cell type, Count per condition per cell type
    p_clr_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "CLR") |>
      ggplot(aes(condition, abundance, color = condition)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = condition_palette) +
      labs(title = "CLR per condition per cell type", x = "", y = "CLR") +
      facet_wrap(~cell_annotation)

    p_count_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype <- .x |>
      filter(metric == "Count") |>
      ggplot(aes(condition, abundance, color = condition)) +
      ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom() +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      scale_color_manual(values = condition_palette) +
      labs(title = "Count per condition per cell type", x = "", y = "Count") +
      facet_wrap(~cell_annotation) +
      ylim(NA, count_99)

    p_abundance_distribution_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype <- (p_clr_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype + p_count_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = paste0("Marker: ", .y)) # .y contains the name of the current marker
    export_plot(
      filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/03_abundance/abundance_plots/per_condition_faceted_by_celltype/{marker_savename}_abundance_distribution_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype")),
      width = 16,
      height = 12,
      plot = p_abundance_distribution_per_condition_faceted_by_celltype
    )
  })
```


# 4. Colocalization score

## 4.1. Heatmap of colocalization score

This section generates colocalization heatmaps that visualize the spatial proximity patterns between marker pairs expressed in the dataset. Colocalization scores quantify the extent to which two markers are found in close proximity to each other within cells, providing insights into protein co-localization and potential molecular interactions or co-expression patterns.

### 4.1.1. Per Group (condition or sample)

For each group (defined by `heatmap_grouping_column`, default: `"condition"`), a heatmap is created showing the mean log2 ratio of observed versus expected colocalization (co-localization score) for expressed marker pairs. The color intensity represents the strength of colocalization (positive values indicate higher-than-expected colocalization, negative values indicate lower-than-expected), while the dot size represents the percentage of cells in which the marker pair was detected. This dual encoding allows simultaneous assessment of both the magnitude and prevalence of colocalization events. The color scale is capped to `c(-1, 1)` to keep the range comparable across experiments.

To keep heatmaps readable when many markers are used, marker display can be limited to the top most abundant (controlled by `max_heatmap_markers`).

To enable direct comparison across groups, all heatmaps use a consistent marker ordering (determined by hierarchical clustering of a reference group) and identical color and size scales. This standardization ensures that differences in colocalization patterns between groups reflect true biological or experimental differences rather than visualization artifacts. Individual heatmaps are saved for each group, and a combined visualization showing all groups side-by-side is also generated to facilitate cross-group comparison.

```{r}
#| label: colocalization_raw_heatmap_per_sample

# Column used to group proximity data for heatmaps. Set to "condition" (default) to
# summarize by experimental condition, or "sample_alias" to summarize per sample.
heatmap_grouping_column <- "condition"

# Maximum number of markers to display in the heatmap. When expressed_markers
# contains more than max_heatmap_markers proteins, they are filtered to the top
# most abundant proteins. Set max_heatmap_markers to Inf to always show all
# expressed markers.
max_heatmap_markers <- 60

expressed_markers <- unique(unlist(markers_to_test))

# Optionally limit markers shown in the heatmap to the top most abundant
plot_markers <-
  head(rowMeans(
    GetAssayData(pg_data, layer = "data")[expressed_markers, , drop = FALSE],
    na.rm = TRUE
  ), max_heatmap_markers) %>%
  names()

proximity_data <- ProximityScores(pg_data,
  lazy = TRUE,
  meta_data_columns = c(heatmap_grouping_column)
) |>
  filter(marker_1 %in% plot_markers) |>
  filter(marker_2 %in% plot_markers) |>
  collect()

summary_proximity_data <- SummarizeProximityScores(proximity_data, group_vars = heatmap_grouping_column)
rm(proximity_data)
gc()

# Create reference heatmap to determine marker ordering
# By default, the reference group is the first one to occur in metadata, but you can specify it explicitly if needed
reference_group <- metadata[[heatmap_grouping_column]][1]
reference_heatmap <- ColocalizationHeatmap(
  summary_proximity_data |>
    filter(.data[[heatmap_grouping_column]] == reference_group),
  marker1_col = "marker_1",
  marker2_col = "marker_2",
  value_col = "mean_log2_ratio",
  size_col = "pct_detected",
  type = "dots",
  cluster_cols = TRUE,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  legend_range = c(-1, 1)
)

marker_order <- layer_scales(reference_heatmap)$y$range$range

# Calculate number of markers for dynamic plot sizing
n_markers <- length(marker_order)

# Calculate plot dimensions based on number of markers
# Base size + scaling factor to ensure readability across different marker counts
# Minimum size ensures small marker sets are still readable, scaling factor accommodates larger sets
base_width <- 6
base_height <- 6
marker_scaling_factor <- 0.15 # Additional inches per marker
plot_width <- max(base_width, base_width + (n_markers - 20) * marker_scaling_factor)
plot_height <- max(base_height, base_height + (n_markers - 20) * marker_scaling_factor)

# Cap the color scale to c(-1, 1) for consistent and readable heatmaps
global_value_limits <- c(-1, 1)

# Calculate global size range across all groups for consistent size scaling
global_size_range <- range(summary_proximity_data$pct_detected, na.rm = TRUE)

# Get all unique group values
unique_groups <- unique(summary_proximity_data[[heatmap_grouping_column]])

# Create heatmaps for each group using the reference marker order
# Store plots in a list to combine them later
group_heatmaps <- list()

for (group in unique_groups) {
  # Filter data for current group
  group_data <- summary_proximity_data |> filter(.data[[heatmap_grouping_column]] == group)

  tmp_plot <- ColocalizationHeatmap(
    group_data,
    marker1_col = "marker_1",
    marker2_col = "marker_2",
    value_col = "mean_log2_ratio",
    size_col = "pct_detected",
    type = "dots",
    cluster_cols = FALSE,
    cluster_rows = FALSE,
    legend_range = global_value_limits # Use capped range for consistent scaling
  ) +
    ggtitle(glue::glue("Raw colocalization heatmap for {group}"))

  # Apply the reference marker order to the ggplot object by modifying the scales
  # This ensures all heatmaps have consistent marker ordering
  tmp_plot <- tmp_plot +
    scale_x_discrete(limits = marker_order, drop = FALSE, position = "top") +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(marker_order), drop = FALSE)

  # Ensure consistent scales across all groups for fair comparison
  # The legend_range parameter already handles the value scale, but we need to ensure
  # the size scale is also consistent. Try both fill and color aesthetics in case
  # ColocalizationHeatmap uses either one
  plot_layers <- tmp_plot$layers
  has_fill <- any(sapply(plot_layers, function(l) "fill" %in% names(l$mapping) || "fill" %in% names(l$aes_params)))
  has_color <- any(sapply(plot_layers, function(l) "colour" %in% names(l$mapping) || "color" %in% names(l$mapping) || "colour" %in% names(l$aes_params)))

  # Apply value scale limits (legend_range should handle this, but ensure it's applied)
  if (has_fill) {
    tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_fill_continuous(limits = global_value_limits, oob = scales::oob_squish)
  }
  if (has_color && !has_fill) {
    tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_color_continuous(limits = global_value_limits, oob = scales::oob_squish)
  }

  # Ensure consistent size scale across all groups
  tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_size_continuous(limits = global_size_range, range = c(0.2, 3))

  # Save individual plot with dimensions scaled to number of markers
  export_plot(
    filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/raw_colocalization_heatmap_per_{heatmap_grouping_column}/{group}_raw_colocalization_heatmap")),
    plot = tmp_plot,
    width = plot_width,
    height = plot_height
  )

  # Store plot for combined visualization
  group_heatmaps[[group]] <- tmp_plot
}

# Create a combined plot with all groups side by side
n_groups <- length(unique_groups)
n_rows <- 2
n_cols <- ceiling(n_groups / n_rows)
combined_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(group_heatmaps, nrow = n_rows)

# Calculate combined plot dimensions: scale width by number of columns, height by number of rows
# Each subplot maintains its aspect ratio while accommodating multiple groups
combined_width <- plot_width * n_cols
combined_height <- plot_height * n_rows

# Save the combined plot
export_plot(
  filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/raw_colocalization_heatmap_per_{heatmap_grouping_column}/all_{heatmap_grouping_column}s_combined_raw_colocalization_heatmap")),
  plot = combined_plot,
  width = combined_width,
  height = combined_height
)
```

### 4.1.2. Per cluster

This section generates cell type-specific colocalization heatmaps, analyzing colocalization patterns separately for each annotated cell type. For each cell type, colocalization heatmaps are created using a set of markers relevant to that specific cell type (defined in `markers_to_test`). The analysis is performed on cells belonging to each cell type separately, then heatmaps are generated for each group (defined by `heatmap_grouping_column`, default: `"condition"`) within that cell type. This enables identification of cell type-specific colocalization patterns and comparison of how these patterns vary across groups within the same cell type.

To keep heatmaps readable when many markers are used, marker display can be limited to the top most abundant proteins (controlled by `max_heatmap_markers`). The color scale is capped to `c(-1, 1)`.

The visualization follows the same principles as the per-group analysis: color intensity represents the mean log2 ratio of observed versus expected colocalization, and dot size indicates the percentage of cells in which the marker pair was detected. All heatmaps for a given cell type use consistent marker ordering and scales to enable direct comparison across groups. Individual heatmaps are saved for each group-cell type combination, and combined visualizations showing all groups side-by-side are generated for each cell type. Results are organized in separate subdirectories for each cell type to facilitate navigation and interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: colocalization_raw_heatmap_per_cell_type

cell_types <- unique(pg_data[[]]$cell_annotation)
cell_types <- cell_types[!is.na(cell_types)]

expressed_markers <- unique(unlist(markers_to_test))

grouped_marker_abundance <-
  FetchData(pg_data,
    vars = c("cell_annotation", expressed_markers),
    layer = "data"
  ) %>%
  group_by(cell_annotation) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(expressed_markers), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  column_to_rownames("cell_annotation")

for (cell_type in cell_types) {
  expressed_markers <- markers_to_test[[cell_type]]

  # Optionally limit markers shown in the heatmap to the top most abundant
  plot_markers <-
    grouped_marker_abundance[cell_type, ] %>%
    unlist() %>%
    sort(decreasing = TRUE) %>%
    head(max_heatmap_markers) %>%
    names()

  pg_data_cell_type <- subset(pg_data, cell_annotation == cell_type)

  proximity_data <- ProximityScores(pg_data_cell_type,
    lazy = TRUE,
    meta_data_columns = c(heatmap_grouping_column)
  ) |>
    filter(marker_1 %in% plot_markers) |>
    filter(marker_2 %in% plot_markers) |>
    collect()

  summary_proximity_data <- SummarizeProximityScores(proximity_data, group_vars = heatmap_grouping_column)
  rm(proximity_data)
  gc()

  # Create reference heatmap to determine marker ordering
  reference_heatmap <- ColocalizationHeatmap(
    summary_proximity_data |>
      group_by(marker_1, marker_2) |>
      summarise(
        mean_log2_ratio = mean(mean_log2_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
        pct_detected = mean(pct_detected, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    marker1_col = "marker_1",
    marker2_col = "marker_2",
    value_col = "mean_log2_ratio",
    size_col = "pct_detected",
    type = "dots",
    cluster_cols = TRUE,
    cluster_rows = TRUE,
    legend_range = c(-1, 1)
  )

  marker_order <- layer_scales(reference_heatmap)$y$range$range

  # Calculate number of markers for dynamic plot sizing
  n_markers <- length(marker_order)

  # Calculate plot dimensions based on number of markers
  # Base size + scaling factor to ensure readability across different marker counts
  # Minimum size ensures small marker sets are still readable, scaling factor accommodates larger sets
  base_width <- 6
  base_height <- 6
  marker_scaling_factor <- 0.15 # Additional inches per marker
  plot_width <- max(base_width, base_width + (n_markers - 20) * marker_scaling_factor)
  plot_height <- max(base_height, base_height + (n_markers - 20) * marker_scaling_factor)

  # Cap the color scale to c(-1, 1) for consistent and readable heatmaps
  global_value_limits <- c(-1, 1)

  # Calculate global size range across all groups for this cell type
  global_size_range <- range(summary_proximity_data$pct_detected, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Get all unique group values
  unique_groups <- unique(summary_proximity_data[[heatmap_grouping_column]])

  # Create heatmaps for each group using the reference marker order
  # Store plots in a list to combine them later
  group_heatmaps <- list()

  for (group in unique_groups) {
    # Filter data for current group
    group_data <-
      summary_proximity_data |>
      filter(.data[[heatmap_grouping_column]] == group)

    if (n_distinct(c(
      group_data$marker_1,
      group_data$marker_2
    )) >= 2) {
      tmp_plot <- ColocalizationHeatmap(
        group_data,
        marker1_col = "marker_1",
        marker2_col = "marker_2",
        value_col = "mean_log2_ratio",
        size_col = "pct_detected",
        type = "dots",
        cluster_cols = FALSE,
        cluster_rows = FALSE,
        legend_range = global_value_limits # Use capped range for consistent scaling
      ) +
        ggtitle(glue::glue("Raw colocalization heatmap for {cell_type} in {group}"))

      # Apply the reference marker order to the ggplot object by modifying the scales
      # This ensures all heatmaps have consistent marker ordering
      tmp_plot <- tmp_plot +
        scale_x_discrete(limits = marker_order, drop = FALSE, position = "top") +
        scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(marker_order), drop = FALSE)

      # Ensure consistent scales across all groups for fair comparison
      # The legend_range parameter already handles the value scale, but we need to ensure
      # the size scale is also consistent. Try both fill and color aesthetics in case
      # ColocalizationHeatmap uses either one
      plot_layers <- tmp_plot$layers
      has_fill <- any(sapply(plot_layers, function(l) "fill" %in% names(l$mapping) || "fill" %in% names(l$aes_params)))
      has_color <- any(sapply(plot_layers, function(l) "colour" %in% names(l$mapping) || "color" %in% names(l$mapping) || "colour" %in% names(l$aes_params)))

      # Apply value scale limits (legend_range should handle this, but ensure it's applied)
      if (has_fill) {
        tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_fill_continuous(limits = global_value_limits, oob = scales::oob_squish)
      }
      if (has_color && !has_fill) {
        tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_color_continuous(limits = global_value_limits, oob = scales::oob_squish)
      }

      # Ensure consistent size scale across all groups
      tmp_plot <- tmp_plot + scale_size_continuous(limits = global_size_range, range = c(0.5, 5))

      # Save individual plot with dimensions scaled to number of markers
      export_plot(
        filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/raw_colocalization_heatmap_per_cell_type/{cell_type}/{group}_{cell_type}_raw_colocalization_heatmap")),
        plot = tmp_plot,
        width = plot_width,
        height = plot_height
      )
    } else {
      # Create an empty plot with a message indicating insufficient markers
      tmp_plot <- ggplot() +
        theme_void() +
        geom_text(aes(0, 0, label = glue::glue("Insufficient markers in {cell_type} for {group}"))) +
        xlim(-1, 1) +
        ylim(-1, 1)
    }

    # Store plot for combined visualization
    group_heatmaps[[group]] <- tmp_plot
  }

  # Create a combined plot with all groups side by side
  n_groups <- length(unique_groups)
  n_rows <- 2
  n_cols <- ceiling(n_groups / n_rows)
  combined_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(group_heatmaps, nrow = n_rows)

  # Calculate combined plot dimensions: scale width by number of columns, height by number of rows
  # Each subplot maintains its aspect ratio while accommodating multiple groups
  combined_width <- plot_width * n_cols
  combined_height <- plot_height * n_rows

  # Save the combined plot
  export_plot(
    filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/raw_colocalization_heatmap_per_cell_type/{cell_type}/{cell_type}_all_{heatmap_grouping_column}s_combined_raw_colocalization_heatmap")),
    plot = combined_plot,
    width = combined_width,
    height = combined_height
  )
}
```


## 4.2. Colocalization Score network

Network visualizations provide an alternative representation of colocalization patterns that can reveal complex relationships and connectivity structures between markers. Unlike heatmaps, which display all pairwise interactions in a matrix format, network graphs focus on the most significant colocalization relationships by filtering based on statistical and biological criteria. This filtering approach helps reduce visual clutter and highlights the most biologically relevant interactions.

In network visualizations, markers are represented as nodes, and colocalization relationships are shown as edges connecting pairs of markers. Edge color encodes the strength of colocalization (mean log2 ratio), while edge width represents the magnitude of the colocalization effect. The network layout algorithm positions nodes to minimize edge crossings and optimize visual clarity, with markers that share similar colocalization patterns tending to cluster together spatially.

The network is constructed by filtering marker pairs based on two key criteria: (1) a minimum colocalization threshold (`metric_threshold`), which can be applied to either positive colocalization only or absolute values, and (2) a minimum detection threshold (`pct_detected_threshold`), ensuring that only marker pairs detected in a sufficient proportion of cells are included. These filters help focus the visualization on robust, biologically meaningful colocalization relationships while reducing noise from weak or rare interactions.

This section provides two complementary analyses: a whole-dataset network visualization that captures global colocalization patterns across all cell types, and cell type-specific network visualizations that reveal how colocalization patterns differ between cell types. Users should select a focused set of markers of interest (`network_markers`) for network visualization, as including too many markers can make the network difficult to interpret.

### 4.2.1. All Cell Types

This section generates network visualizations that capture colocalization patterns across all cell types in the dataset, with separate network plots created for each group (defined by `network_grouping_column`, default: condition). This whole-dataset approach provides a global view of marker colocalization relationships and enables comparison of how these relationships vary across conditions. The analysis includes all cells regardless of cell type annotation, making it useful for identifying condition-specific colocalization patterns and detecting potential batch effects or experimental condition-specific changes. Set `network_grouping_column` to `"sample_alias"` to facet by individual sample.

Users should specify a focused set of `network_markers` for visualization, as network graphs become difficult to interpret with too many nodes. The filtering thresholds (`metric_threshold` and `pct_detected_threshold`) help focus the visualization on the most robust colocalization relationships. The `only_positive_mean_log2_ratio` parameter can be set to filter for only positive colocalization (markers that co-occur more frequently than expected) or to include both positive and negative colocalization relationships.

```{r}
#| label: colocalization_score_network_all_cell_types

# Column used to facet network plots. Set to "condition" (default) to facet by
# experimental condition, or "sample_alias" to facet by individual sample.
network_grouping_column <- "condition"

network_markers <- c("CD52", "CD59", "CD81", "CD82", "CD43", "CD44", "CD45", "CD45RA", "CD45RB", "CD8")
only_positive_mean_log2_ratio <- TRUE
# Define the threshold for the metric and the percentage of detected cells - this will be used to filter the data for the network plot
metric_threshold <- 0.1
pct_detected_threshold <- 0.5

proximity_data <- ProximityScores(pg_data,
  lazy = TRUE,
  meta_data_columns = c(network_grouping_column)
) |>
  filter(marker_1 %in% network_markers) |>
  filter(marker_2 %in% network_markers) |>
  collect()

summary_proximity_data <- SummarizeProximityScores(proximity_data, group_vars = network_grouping_column)
rm(proximity_data)
gc()

# Create the network plot: filter the data for the network plot based on the metric and the percentage of detected cells, then create the network plot - this is also where you can include additional filtering options, such as for example to only include positive mean_log2_ratio.
df_net <- summary_proximity_data %>%
  filter(if (only_positive_mean_log2_ratio) mean_log2_ratio > metric_threshold else abs(mean_log2_ratio) > metric_threshold) %>%
  filter(pct_detected > pct_detected_threshold) %>%
  mutate(from = marker_1, to = marker_2) %>%
  select(from, to, mean_log2_ratio, !!sym(network_grouping_column))

tidygraph::as_tbl_graph(df_net) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "kk") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(color = mean_log2_ratio, width = abs(mean_log2_ratio))) +
  geom_node_label(aes(label = name), size = 2.5) +
  scale_edge_color_gradientn(
    colours = gradient_palette,
    limits = c(-1, 1) * abs(max(df_net$mean_log2_ratio))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.2, 0.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.2, 0.2)) +
  facet_edges(as.formula(paste0("~", network_grouping_column)), nrow = 2) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  ) +
  labs(edge_color = "Mean\nlog2 ratio", title = "Colocalization Score Network All Cell Types", subtitle = glue::glue("Metric threshold{if (only_positive_mean_log2_ratio) ' (only positive)' else ' (absolute value)'}: {metric_threshold}, Percentage of cells above threshold: {pct_detected_threshold}")) +
  guides(edge_width = "none")

export_plot(
  filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/colocalization_score_network/colocalization_score_network_all_cell_types/all_cell_types_colocalization_score_network")),
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)
```


### 4.2.2. Per Cell Type

This section generates cell type-specific network visualizations, analyzing colocalization patterns within a single cell type of interest. By focusing on a specific cell type, this analysis can reveal cell type-specific colocalization signatures that may be masked in whole-dataset analyses. The network visualization helps identify which markers form strong colocalization relationships within the selected cell type and how these relationships vary across groups (defined by `network_grouping_column`, default: condition). Set `network_grouping_column` to `"sample_alias"` to facet by individual sample.

Users should specify the `cell_type_of_interest` variable to select which cell type to analyze. The same filtering criteria and visualization principles apply as in the all-cell-types analysis, but the proximity data is filtered to include only cells belonging to the specified cell type. This enables identification of cell type-specific marker interactions and comparison of how colocalization networks differ between cell types.

```{r}
#| label: colocalization_score_network_per_cell_type

network_markers <- c("CD52", "CD59", "CD81", "CD82", "CD43", "CD44", "CD45", "CD45RA", "CD45RB", "CD8")
cell_type_of_interest <- "CD8 T"
only_positive_mean_log2_ratio <- TRUE
# Define the threshold for the metric and the percentage of detected cells - this will be used to filter the data for the network plot
metric_threshold <- 0.1
pct_detected_threshold <- 0.5

proximity_data <- ProximityScores(pg_data,
  lazy = TRUE,
  meta_data_columns = c(network_grouping_column, "cell_annotation")
) |>
  filter(cell_annotation == cell_type_of_interest) |>
  filter(marker_1 %in% network_markers) |>
  filter(marker_2 %in% network_markers) |>
  filter(marker_1 != marker_2) |>
  collect()

summary_proximity_data <- SummarizeProximityScores(proximity_data, group_vars = network_grouping_column)
rm(proximity_data)
gc()

# Create the network plot: filter the data for the network plot based on the metric and the percentage of detected cells, then create the network plot - this is also where you can include additional filtering options, such as for example to only include positive mean_log2_ratio.
df_net <- summary_proximity_data %>%
  filter(if (only_positive_mean_log2_ratio) mean_log2_ratio > metric_threshold else abs(mean_log2_ratio) > metric_threshold) %>%
  filter(pct_detected > pct_detected_threshold) %>%
  mutate(from = marker_1, to = marker_2) %>%
  select(from, to, mean_log2_ratio, !!sym(network_grouping_column))

tidygraph::as_tbl_graph(df_net) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "kk") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(color = mean_log2_ratio, width = abs(mean_log2_ratio))) +
  geom_node_label(aes(label = name), size = 2.5) +
  scale_edge_color_gradientn(
    colours = gradient_palette,
    limits = c(-abs(max(df_net$mean_log2_ratio)), abs(max(df_net$mean_log2_ratio)))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.2, 0.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.2, 0.2)) +
  facet_edges(as.formula(paste0("~", network_grouping_column)), nrow = 2) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  ) +
  labs(
    edge_color = "Mean\nlog2 ratio",
    title = glue::glue("Colocalization Score Network {cell_type_of_interest}"),
    subtitle = glue::glue(
      "Metric threshold{if (only_positive_mean_log2_ratio) ' (only positive)' else ' (absolute value)'}: {metric_threshold}, Percentage of cells above threshold: {pct_detected_threshold}"
    )
  ) +
  guides(edge_width = "none")

export_plot(
  filename = glue::glue(here::here("results/04_raw_proximity/colocalization_score_network/colocalization_score_network_per_cell_type/{cell_type_of_interest}/{cell_type_of_interest}_colocalization_score_network")),
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)
```




# 5. Statistical testing

## 5.0. Set reference sample

By default, in this analysis we compare all conditions to a reference condition, which is typically the "resting" or "control" condition. This allows us to identify markers that are differentially abundant or spatially clustered or colocalized in stimulated or treated conditions compared to the baseline state. 

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_set_reference

reference_condition <- "resting"

if (!reference_condition %in% metadata$condition) stop("The reference condition is not present in the sample metadata")
```


## 5.1. Differential abundance analysis

Differential abundance analysis identifies markers that exhibit statistically significant differences in expression levels between experimental conditions. This analysis is essential for understanding how experimental treatments, disease states, or other conditions affect protein expression patterns within specific cell types.

The analysis is performed separately for each annotated cell type, comparing marker abundance between a target condition (e.g., stimulated, treated) and a reference condition (e.g., resting, control). For each marker within each cell type, a statistical test (typically the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, also known as the Mann-Whitney U test) is used to assess whether the distribution of marker abundance differs significantly between conditions. The Wilcoxon test is a non-parametric test that does not assume normal distribution of the data, making it robust for single-cell data which often exhibits non-normal distributions and high variability.

The test compares marker expression values (typically CLR-normalized values) between cells in the target condition versus cells in the reference condition. For each marker, the analysis reports an effect size (typically the difference in mean or median expression) and a p-value indicating the statistical significance of the difference. Multiple testing correction is applied using the false discovery rate (FDR) method to control for the large number of statistical tests performed across multiple markers and cell types.

Results are organized by cell type and include both the raw statistical outputs and summary visualizations. Markers with significant differences (typically p_adj < 0.05) and large effect sizes are of particular biological interest, as they represent markers whose expression is substantially altered by the experimental condition. This analysis enables identification of condition-specific markers, understanding of cellular responses to treatments, and discovery of biomarkers associated with different experimental states.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_abundance_analysis

differential_abundance_analysis <-
  names(markers_to_test) |>
  map(function(x) {
    tryCatch(
      {
        daa_res <- RunDAA(subset(pg_data, cell_annotation == x),
          contrast_column = "condition",
          reference = reference_condition,
          features = markers_to_test[[x]]
        )
        daa_res$group <- x
        return(daa_res)
      },
      error = function(e) {
        message(paste("Error for cell type:", x, ":", e))
        return(NULL)
      }
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "fdr")) # recalculate the adjusted p values after multiple testing correction for all comparisons, not only per cell type

dir.create(here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/abundance"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a file
saveRDS(differential_abundance_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/abundance/differential_abundance_analysis.rds"))

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a csv file
write.csv(differential_abundance_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/abundance/differential_abundance_analysis.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```    

### 5.1.1. Summarizing plots

Here we create two types of summarizing plots for the differential abundance analysis results:

1. **Volcano plot**: Shows the relationship between effect size (log fold change) and statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value) for each marker, faceted by cell type. This helps identify markers that are both significantly different and have large effect sizes.

2. **Heatmap**: Displays significant markers (adjusted p-value < 0.05) across all cell types, with colors representing the effect size. This provides an overview of which markers are differentially abundant in which cell types.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_abundance_plots

# Determine the effect size column name
effect_size_col <- "difference"

# Determine the feature/marker column name
feature_col <- "marker"

# Determine target conditions - check if dataframe has target/contrast columns
if ("target" %in% colnames(differential_abundance_analysis)) {
  # If target column exists, get all unique targets
  target_conditions <- unique(differential_abundance_analysis$target)
  target_conditions <- target_conditions[!is.na(target_conditions)]
} else {
  stop("Could not find target column. Available columns: ", paste(colnames(differential_abundance_analysis), collapse = ", "))
}

# Prepare base data for plotting (add target column if it doesn't exist)
# p_adj values of zero (floating-point underflow) are coerced to
# min_p_value_threshold before the -log10 transform to prevent Inf values
# that would clip data-point labels in volcano plots.
plot_data_base <- differential_abundance_analysis |>
  mutate(
    neg_log10_p_adj = -log10(pmax(p_adj, min_p_value_threshold)),
    significant = p_adj < 0.05,
    effect_size = !!sym(effect_size_col),
    marker = !!sym(feature_col)
  )


# Loop through each target condition and create plots
for (target_condition in target_conditions) {
  # Filter data for this target (if target column exists)
  if ("target" %in% colnames(plot_data_base)) {
    plot_data <- plot_data_base |>
      filter(target == target_condition)
  }

  # Skip if no data for this target
  if (nrow(plot_data) == 0) {
    warning(paste("No data found for target condition:", target_condition))
    next
  }

  # Create directory name based on target and reference
  comparison_dir <- paste0(target_condition, "_vs_", reference_condition)
  base_output_dir <- here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/abundance/differential_abundance_plots", comparison_dir)

  # Plot 1: Volcano plot showing effect size vs significance, faceted by cell type
  # This plot helps identify markers that are both significantly different and have large effect sizes
  # Identify top 5 most extreme effect sizes per cell type for labeling
  top_markers_faceted <- plot_data |>
    group_by(group) |>
    slice_max(order_by = abs(effect_size), n = 5) |>
    ungroup()

  volcano_plot_differential_abundance <-
    plot_data |>
    ggplot(aes(x = effect_size, y = neg_log10_p_adj, color = effect_size)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), col = "grey") +
    geom_text(
      data = top_markers_faceted,
      aes(label = marker),
      hjust = 0.5,
      vjust = -0.5,
      size = 2
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free") +
    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = c(min(plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE), max(plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE)),
      expand = expansion(0.1)
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))
    ) +
    scale_color_gradientn(
      colors = gradient_palette,
      limits = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(plot_data$effect_size), na.rm = TRUE)
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Differential abundance analysis: Volcano plot (", target_condition, " vs ", reference_condition, ")", sep = ""),
      subtitle = "Effect size vs statistical significance by cell type",
      x = paste("Effect size (", effect_size_col, ")", sep = ""),
      y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
      color = "Effect size"
    )

  # Save faceted volcano plot in the comparison directory
  export_plot(
    filename = file.path(base_output_dir, "differential_abundance_volcano"),
    plot = volcano_plot_differential_abundance,
    width = 12,
    height = 8
  )

  # Plot 2: Non-faceted volcano plots per cell type
  # Create individual folders per cell type and save non-faceted volcano plots for each cell type
  # Get unique cell types (groups)
  unique_cell_types <- unique(plot_data$group)

  # For each cell type, create a non-faceted volcano plot
  for (cell_type in unique_cell_types) {
    # Create directory for this cell type
    cell_type_dir <- file.path(base_output_dir, cell_type)
    dir.create(cell_type_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

    # Filter data for this cell type
    cell_type_plot_data <- plot_data |>
      filter(group == cell_type)

    # Create non-faceted volcano plot for this cell type
    # Identify top 5 most extreme effect sizes for labeling
    top_markers_cell_type <- cell_type_plot_data |>
      slice_max(order_by = abs(effect_size), n = 5)

    volcano_plot_cell_type <-
      cell_type_plot_data |>
      ggplot(aes(x = effect_size, y = neg_log10_p_adj, color = effect_size)) +
      geom_point(size = 0.5) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), col = "grey") +
      geom_text(
        data = top_markers_cell_type,
        aes(label = marker),
        hjust = 0.5,
        vjust = -0.5,
        size = 3
      ) +
      facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free") +
      scale_x_continuous(
        limits = c(
          min(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE),
          max(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE)
        ),
        expand = expansion(0.1)
      ) +
      scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))
      ) +
      scale_color_gradientn(
        colors = gradient_palette,
        limits = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size), na.rm = TRUE)
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(
        panel.grid = element_blank()
      ) +
      labs(
        title = paste("Differential abundance analysis: Volcano plot", sep = ""),
        subtitle = paste("Cell type: ", cell_type, " (", target_condition, " vs ", reference_condition, ")", sep = ""),
        x = paste("Effect size (", effect_size_col, ")", sep = ""),
        y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
        color = "Effect size"
      )

    # Save non-faceted volcano plot
    export_plot(
      filename = file.path(cell_type_dir, "volcano_plot"),
      plot = volcano_plot_cell_type,
      width = 5.5,
      height = 4.5
    )
  }

  # Plot 3: Heatmap showing significant markers across cell types
  # This provides an overview of which markers are differentially abundant in which cell types
  # Filter for significant markers and prepare data for heatmap
  significant_markers <-
    plot_data |>
    group_by(marker) |>
    filter(any(significant) & any(abs(effect_size) > 0.5)) |>
    select(marker, group, effect_size) |>
    # Pivot to wide format for heatmap
    pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = effect_size, values_fill = 0) |>
    column_to_rownames("marker") |>
    as.matrix()

  # Only create heatmap if there are significant markers
  if (nrow(significant_markers) > 0 && ncol(significant_markers) > 0) {
    # Determine color scale breaks based on robust data range (use 1st and 99th percentiles to reduce outlier influence)
    effect_vals <- as.numeric(significant_markers)
    effect_quantiles <- quantile(effect_vals, probs = c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
    max_abs_effect <- max(abs(effect_quantiles))
    breaks_range <- seq(-max_abs_effect, max_abs_effect, length.out = 101)

    heatmap_differential_abundance <-
      significant_markers |>
      t() |>
      pheatmap(
        color = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry"),
        breaks = breaks_range,
        cellwidth = 8,
        cellheight = 8,
        cluster_rows = TRUE,
        cluster_cols = TRUE,
        heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "Effect size"),
        fontsize = 8
      ) |>
      as.ggplot()

    export_plot(
      filename = file.path(base_output_dir, "differential_abundance_heatmap"),
      plot = heatmap_differential_abundance,

      # ~0.3 in per marker column + 4 in base margin; ~0.5 in per cell-type row + 2 in base margin.
      width = max(6, nrow(significant_markers) * 0.15 + 1.5),
      height = max(4, ncol(significant_markers) * 0.2 + 1.5)
    )
  } else {
    warning(paste("No significant markers found for heatmap visualization (p_adj < 0.05) for", target_condition, "vs", reference_condition))
  }
}
```

## 5.2. Differential Clustering Analysis

Differential clustering analysis identifies markers that exhibit statistically significant differences in spatial clustering patterns between experimental conditions. In this context, "clustering" refers to the spatial aggregation of a marker with itself—that is, the extent to which a marker tends to form clusters or aggregates within cells rather than being uniformly distributed.

The analysis is performed separately for each cell type, comparing clustering patterns between target and reference conditions. A statistical test (typically the Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is used to assess whether the distribution of clustering scores (log2 ratio of observed versus expected self-proximity) differs significantly between conditions. Multiple testing correction is applied using FDR to control for the number of statistical tests performed across markers and cell types.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_proximity

differential_clustering_analysis <-
  names(markers_to_test) |>
  map(function(x) {
    tryCatch(
      {
        # Store markers in a variable to ensure proper evaluation in lazy query context
        # Convert to character vector to ensure proper SQL translation
        markers_vec <- as.character(markers_to_test[[x]])
        proximity_data <- ProximityScores(subset(pg_data, cell_annotation == x),
          lazy = TRUE,
          meta_data_columns = c("sample_alias", "condition")
        ) |>
          filter(marker_1 == marker_2) |>
          filter(marker_1 %in% markers_vec) |>
          filter(marker_2 %in% markers_vec) |>
          collect()

        res <- DifferentialProximityAnalysis(proximity_data,
          contrast_column = "condition",
          reference = reference_condition,
          proximity_metric = "log2_ratio",
          min_n_obs = 5
        )
        res$group <- x
        return(res)
      },
      error = function(e) {
        message(paste("Error for cell type:", x, ":", e))
        return(NULL)
      }
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "fdr")) # recalculate the adjusted p values after multiple testing correction for all comparisons, not only per cell type

dir.create(here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/clustering"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a file
saveRDS(differential_clustering_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/clustering/differential_clustering_analysis.rds"))

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a csv file
write.csv(differential_clustering_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/clustering/differential_clustering_analysis.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```


### 5.2.1. Summarizing plots

Here we create two types of summarizing plots for the differential clustering analysis results:

1. **Volcano plot**: Shows the relationship between effect size (log fold change) and statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value) for each marker, faceted by cell type. This helps identify markers that are both significantly different and have large effect sizes.

2. **Heatmap**: Displays significant markers (adjusted p-value < 0.05) across all cell types, with colors representing the effect size. This provides an overview of which markers are differentially clustered in which cell types.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_clustering_plots

# Determine the effect size column name
effect_size_col <- "diff_median"

# Determine the feature/marker column name
feature_col <- "marker_1"

# Determine target conditions - check if dataframe has target/contrast columns
if ("target" %in% colnames(differential_clustering_analysis)) {
  # If target column exists, get all unique targets
  target_conditions <- unique(differential_clustering_analysis$target)
  target_conditions <- target_conditions[!is.na(target_conditions)]
} else {
  stop("Could not find target column. Available columns: ", paste(colnames(differential_clustering_analysis), collapse = ", "))
}

# Prepare base data for plotting (add target column if it doesn't exist)
# p_adj values of zero are coerced to min_p_value_threshold before the
# -log10 transform to prevent Inf values that would clip data-point labels.
plot_data_base <- differential_clustering_analysis |>
  mutate(
    neg_log10_p_adj = -log10(pmax(p_adj, min_p_value_threshold)),
    significant = p_adj < 0.05,
    effect_size = !!sym(effect_size_col),
    marker = !!sym(feature_col)
  )


# Loop through each target condition and create plots
for (target_condition in target_conditions) {
  # Filter data for this target (if target column exists)
  if ("target" %in% colnames(plot_data_base)) {
    plot_data <- plot_data_base |>
      filter(target == target_condition)
  }

  # Skip if no data for this target
  if (nrow(plot_data) == 0) {
    warning(paste("No data found for target condition:", target_condition))
    next
  }

  # Create directory name based on target and reference
  comparison_dir <- paste0(target_condition, "_vs_", reference_condition)
  base_output_dir <- here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/clustering/differential_clustering_plots", comparison_dir)

  # Plot 1: Volcano plot showing effect size vs significance, faceted by cell type
  # This plot helps identify markers that are both significantly different and have large effect sizes
  # Identify top 5 most extreme effect sizes per cell type for labeling
  top_markers_faceted <- plot_data |>
    group_by(group) |>
    slice_max(order_by = abs(effect_size), n = 5) |>
    ungroup()

  volcano_plot_differential_clustering <-
    plot_data |>
    ggplot(aes(x = effect_size, y = neg_log10_p_adj, color = effect_size)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), col = "grey") +
    geom_text(
      data = top_markers_faceted,
      aes(label = marker),
      hjust = 0.5,
      vjust = -0.5,
      size = 2
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free") +
    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = c(min(plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE), max(plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE)),
      expand = expansion(0.1)
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))
    ) +
    scale_color_gradientn(
      colors = gradient_palette,
      limits = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(plot_data$effect_size), na.rm = TRUE)
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Differential clustering analysis: Volcano plot (", target_condition, " vs ", reference_condition, ")", sep = ""),
      subtitle = "Effect size vs statistical significance by cell type",
      x = paste("Effect size (", effect_size_col, ")", sep = ""),
      y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
      color = "Effect size"
    )

  # Save faceted volcano plot in the comparison directory
  export_plot(
    filename = file.path(base_output_dir, "differential_clustering_volcano"),
    plot = volcano_plot_differential_clustering,
    width = 12,
    height = 8
  )

  # Plot 2: Non-faceted volcano plots per cell type
  # Create individual folders per cell type and save non-faceted volcano plots for each cell type
  # Get unique cell types (groups)
  unique_cell_types <- unique(plot_data$group)

  # For each cell type, create a non-faceted volcano plot
  for (cell_type in unique_cell_types) {
    # Create directory for this cell type
    cell_type_dir <- file.path(base_output_dir, cell_type)
    dir.create(cell_type_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

    # Filter data for this cell type
    cell_type_plot_data <- plot_data |>
      filter(group == cell_type)

    # Create non-faceted volcano plot for this cell type
    # Identify top 5 most extreme effect sizes for labeling
    top_markers_cell_type <- cell_type_plot_data |>
      slice_max(order_by = abs(effect_size), n = 5)

    volcano_plot_cell_type <-
      cell_type_plot_data |>
      ggplot(aes(x = effect_size, y = neg_log10_p_adj, color = effect_size)) +
      geom_point(size = 0.5) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), col = "grey") +
      geom_text(
        data = top_markers_cell_type,
        aes(label = marker),
        hjust = 0.5,
        vjust = -0.5,
        size = 3
      ) +
      facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free") +
      scale_x_continuous(
        limits = c(
          min(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE),
          max(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE)
        ),
        expand = expansion(0.1)
      ) +
      scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))
      ) +
      scale_color_gradientn(
        colors = gradient_palette,
        limits = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(cell_type_plot_data$effect_size), na.rm = TRUE)
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(
        panel.grid = element_blank()
      ) +
      labs(
        title = paste("Differential clustering analysis: Volcano plot", sep = ""),
        subtitle = paste("Cell type: ", cell_type, " (", target_condition, " vs ", reference_condition, ")", sep = ""),
        x = paste("Effect size (", effect_size_col, ")", sep = ""),
        y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
        color = "Effect size"
      )

    # Save non-faceted volcano plot
    export_plot(
      filename = file.path(cell_type_dir, "volcano_plot"),
      plot = volcano_plot_cell_type,
      width = 5.5,
      height = 4.5
    )
  }

  # Plot 3: Heatmap showing significant markers across cell types
  # This provides an overview of which markers are differentially clustered in which cell types
  # Filter for significant markers and prepare data for heatmap
  significant_markers <-
    plot_data |>
    group_by(marker) |>
    filter(any(significant) & any(abs(effect_size) > 0.5)) |>
    select(marker, group, effect_size) |>
    # Pivot to wide format for heatmap
    pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = effect_size, values_fill = 0) |>
    column_to_rownames("marker") |>
    as.matrix()

  # Only create heatmap if there are significant markers
  if (nrow(significant_markers) > 0 && ncol(significant_markers) > 0) {
    # Determine color scale breaks based on robust data range (use 1st and 99th percentiles to reduce outlier influence)
    effect_vals <- as.numeric(significant_markers)
    effect_quantiles <- quantile(effect_vals, probs = c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
    max_abs_effect <- max(abs(effect_quantiles))
    breaks_range <- seq(-max_abs_effect, max_abs_effect, length.out = 101)

    heatmap_differential_clustering <-
      significant_markers |>
      t() |>
      pheatmap(
        color = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry"),
        breaks = breaks_range,
        cellwidth = 8,
        cellheight = 8,
        cluster_rows = TRUE,
        cluster_cols = TRUE,
        heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "Effect size"),
        fontsize = 8
      ) |>
      as.ggplot()

    export_plot(
      filename = file.path(base_output_dir, "differential_clustering_heatmap"),
      plot = heatmap_differential_clustering,

      # ~0.3 in per marker column + 4 in base margin; ~0.5 in per cell-type row + 2 in base margin.
      width = max(6, nrow(significant_markers) * 0.15 + 1.5),
      height = max(4, ncol(significant_markers) * 0.2 + 1.5)
    )
  } else {
    warning(paste("No significant markers found for heatmap visualization (p_adj < 0.05) for", target_condition, "vs", reference_condition))
  }
}
```

## 5.3. Differential Colocalization Analysis

Differential colocalization analysis identifies markers that exhibit statistically significant differences in spatial proximity patterns between experimental conditions. The analysis is performed separately for each cell type, comparing colocalization patterns between target and reference conditions. A statistical test is used to assess whether the distribution of colocalization scores (log2 ratio of observed versus expected proximity) differs significantly between conditions. Multiple testing correction is applied using FDR to control for the number of statistical tests performed across markers and cell types.


```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_colocalization


differential_colocalization_analysis <-
  names(markers_to_test) |>
  map(function(x) {
    tryCatch(
      {
        # Store markers in a variable to ensure proper evaluation in lazy query context
        # Convert to character vector to ensure proper SQL translation
        markers_vec <- as.character(markers_to_test[[x]])
        proximity_data <- ProximityScores(subset(pg_data, cell_annotation == x),
          lazy = TRUE,
          meta_data_columns = c("sample_alias", "condition")
        ) |>
          filter(marker_1 %in% markers_vec) |>
          filter(marker_2 %in% markers_vec) |>
          collect()

        res <- DifferentialProximityAnalysis(proximity_data,
          contrast_column = "condition",
          reference = reference_condition,
          proximity_metric = "log2_ratio",
          min_n_obs = 5
        )
        res$group <- x
        return(res)
      },
      error = function(e) {
        message(paste("Error for cell type:", x, ":", e))
        return(NULL)
      }
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "fdr")) # recalculate the adjusted p values after multiple testing correction for all comparisons, not only per cell type

dir.create(here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/colocalization"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a file
saveRDS(differential_colocalization_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/colocalization/differential_colocalization_analysis.rds"))

# Save the differential abundance analysis results to a csv file
write.csv(differential_colocalization_analysis, here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/colocalization/differential_colocalization_analysis.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

### 5.3.1. Summarizing plots

Here we create summarizing plots for the differential colocalization analysis results:

1. **Colocalization Heatmap**: Displays the difference in medians for marker pairs, with dot size representing statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value). This provides an overview of which marker pairs are differentially colocalized for each cell type and condition comparison.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_differential_colocalization_plot

# Determine target conditions - check if dataframe has target/contrast columns
if ("target" %in% colnames(differential_colocalization_analysis)) {
  # If target column exists, get all unique targets
  target_conditions <- unique(differential_colocalization_analysis$target)
  target_conditions <- target_conditions[!is.na(target_conditions)]
} else {
  stop("Could not find target column. Available columns: ", paste(colnames(differential_colocalization_analysis), collapse = ", "))
}

# Get unique cell types (groups)
unique_cell_types <- unique(differential_colocalization_analysis$group)
unique_cell_types <- unique_cell_types[!is.na(unique_cell_types)]

# Loop through each target condition and cell type combination
for (target_condition in target_conditions) {
  # Create directory name based on target and reference
  comparison_dir <- paste0(target_condition, "_vs_", reference_condition)
  base_output_dir <- here::here("results/05_statistical_testing/colocalization/differential_colocalization_plots", comparison_dir)

  for (cell_type in unique_cell_types) {
    # Create directory for this cell type
    cell_type_dir <- file.path(base_output_dir, cell_type)
    dir.create(cell_type_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

    # Filter data for this target and cell type
    # Set diff_median to 0 for non-significant results (p_adj >= 0.001) to focus on highly significant changes
    plot_data <-
      differential_colocalization_analysis %>%
      filter(group == cell_type & target == target_condition)

    plot_markers <-
      plot_data %>%
      filter(p_adj < 0.001) %>%
      select(marker_1, marker_2) %>%
      deframe() %>%
      unique() %>%
      head(14)

    plot_data <-
      plot_data %>%
      filter(
        marker_1 %in% plot_markers,
        marker_2 %in% plot_markers
      )

    # Skip if no data for this combination
    if (nrow(plot_data) == 0) {
      warning(paste("No data found for target condition:", target_condition, "and cell type:", cell_type))
      next
    }

    # Create the colocalization heatmap plot
    # Add title indicating the target and cell type
    colocalization_heatmap <-
      ColocalizationHeatmap(
        plot_data,
        marker1_col = "marker_1",
        marker2_col = "marker_2",
        value_col = "diff_median",
        type = "dots",
        colors = gradient_palette,
        size_col_transform = \(x) {
          -log10(x)
        }
      ) &
        labs(size = "-log10(p_adj)") &
        scale_size(range = c(1, 5), limits = c(0, max(-log10(plot_data$p_adj)))) &
        labs(fill = "Difference\nin medians") &
        labs(
          title = paste("Differential Colocalization Analysis", sep = ""),
          subtitle = paste("Cell type: ", cell_type, " (", target_condition, " vs ", reference_condition, ")", sep = "")
        )

    # Save the plot
    export_plot(
      filename = file.path(cell_type_dir, "colocalization_heatmap"),
      plot = colocalization_heatmap,
      width = max(c(4, length(plot_markers) * 0.15 + 1.5)),
      height = max(c(4, length(plot_markers) * 0.15 + 3))
    )
  }
}
```
